Canada Drops Other Hemp Shoe – Ends 60 Year Ban On Hemp Cultivation
Meanwhile in DEAland, Hope in Vermont?

As expected, Friday the 13th turned out to be an unlucky day for prohibitionists when the Canadian Health Minister Allan Rock issued regulations permitting the cultivation of industrial hemp for the first time in 60 years. Rock even said, ``This new crop has a tremendous potential for creating new jobs in agriculture, industry, research and retail."

Canadian farmers with special research licenses have been producing small quantities of hemp, but not for commercial purposes. Industrial hemp grown in Canada must meet the European Union standard of having less than .03% THC. He said Health Canada will issue licenses, permits and authorizations to control activities under the Industrial Hemp Regulations.

An official statement said, ``Importers, exporters, distributors, growers and processors will be required to apply for and maintain a license or permit to carry out any activities authorized under the regulations... This level of control is necessary to prevent the diversion of Cannabis to the illicit drug market.''

``The government has thrown the challenge back to us to truly develop hemp as a viable resource in Canada, said Geof Kime, the President of Ontario's Hempline Inc., whose company broke the hemp growing prohibition in North America in 1994 after being granted a special growing license.

``We will soon be moving forward into full commercial production and exporting to the U.S. textile industry,'' Kime said. ``The announcement will pave the way to allow Canada to become a global leader in the hemp industry.''

Kime's company currently farms only 10 acres of hemp, a far cry from the estimated 100,000 acres being cultivated in the European Union in 1998-99.

There is substantial evidence that there is a very large and rapidly expanding market for Canadian hemp products. All of the hemp used in the US must be imported from China or Europe, so Canadian hemp will enjoy a significant freight advantage over these producers. Inasmuch as many hemp products are bulky, this could be very important.

For example, there was testimony Friday before a Vermont State Senate committee that if Vermont farmers were allowed to grow industrial hemp, there are mills in Maine and Massachusetts ready to process it. Raymond A. Berard, a carpet company executive from Georgia told the Vermont Senate Agriculture Committee that Interface Research Corp. in Kennesaw, Ga., is already processing hemp fiber from Canada at some of its mills around the United States and elsewhere.

The carpet maker, which does $1.2 billion in business a year, now buys its hemp in China and Hungary and from farmers growing test plots in Canada. If U.S. producers were allowed to grow hemp, Interface could buy as much as they could grow, Berard said.

``We're not talking tiny volumes here,'' Berard said. ``We'd buy several million pounds a year. You couldn't grow enough hemp in Vermont.''

The Governor of Vermont follows the DEA line and is expected to veto the bill that would allow some farmers to grow supervised test plots of the hemp plant.
See Vermonters Wrestle with Legalizing Hemp. Many ask, "Why is Governor Dean Afraid of a Plant?"

Netaka J. White, who owns a hemp products company in Middlebury, told the committee that the marijuana argument was ``a war of words.

``A lot of the controversy is a campaign of language ... The terming of cannabis as marijuana plays on our collective fears,'' said White, who came to testify in hemp pants and a hemp shirt and blazer. ``It's been waged in Vermont and on a national level.''

``I agree with you,'' said Sen. Cheryl Rivers, D-Windsor, a member of the committee. ``I think when law enforcement does that, they undermine their credibility.''

Berard brought some samples of carpet made with hemp fiber and a hemp backing when he testified Friday. His company is looking for a natural product that can be recycled or used for compost instead of the nylon it now uses for most of its carpets, he said. Hemp fits the criteria.

``I've been studying hemp for three years,'' said Berard. ``Hemp is the strongest fiber I've found. We expect carpet to last for 10 years; it's not easy to find a natural fiber that does that.''

Berard and White asked the committee to support the legislation and to promote the growing of industrial hemp. Pressure from the states will persuade federal policymakers to change their stance on the plant, Berard said.

``This is a real opportunity to educate people on the benefits of hemp,'' White said.

Sen. Sara Brannon Kittell, the chairwoman of the committee, said she believed if there was money to be made with hemp, farmers should be allowed to try it.

``I think the market is growing some, so I think we should be looking at it, and not listening to the campaign of words,'' she said after the hearing.

The DEA and other prohibitionists claim that marijuana used in the 1960’s only had the same low level of THC as industrial hemp and that the industrial hemp movement -- like the medical marijuana movement -- is really just a front for NORML and a secret cabal of multimillionaires who want to legalize all drugs.

The DEA also claims that -- unlike their counterparts in Canada, France, the UK and many other countries -- American police simply are not smart enough to be able to tell the difference between a tall thin stalk of hemp and a large bushy marijuana plant with flowers. It is not known whether this position is based on double-blind tests of US and foreign police or is merely based on anecdotal evidence.
See A Kentucky Prohibitionist’s View of The Industrial Hemp Conspiracy To Legalize Marijuana

Richard Cowan
